idiom_name: Data.define values with with(...) and case/in; the shell is the script
implementation_notes: `Data.define` gives frozen, equality-by-value objects with `with(...)` for non-destructive updates and `case/in` pattern matching for the decision space, so the core is a module of pure methods that take and return `Data` instances and never open a file, hit the database or call `Time.now`; the shell (a `bin/` script, a Rake task, a Sinatra route) reads the world, calls the core and carries out the decision. That replaces the classic domain-object-per-rule design with injected collaborators, which is worth keeping only when the decisions are large enough to be objects themselves. Freezing is shallow and `Struct` stays mutable, so value discipline is a convention: `# frozen_string_literal: true`, no ivar mutation, time and ids passed in.
code_sketch:
Quote = Data.define(:subtotal, :tax, :total)

def price(items, promo:, now:)          # pure core
  subtotal = items.sum { |i| i.unit_cents * i.qty }
  subtotal = subtotal * 90 / 100 if promo
  Quote.new(subtotal:, tax: subtotal / 10, total: subtotal + subtotal / 10)
end

# shell: read -> decide -> write
order = OrderRepo.find(id)
quote = price(order.items, promo: Flags.promo?(order.user_id), now: Time.now)
OrderRepo.save_quote(order.id, quote)
pitfalls: `Data` members are frozen but shallow: an Array/Hash member can still be mutated in place, after which the object's hash and equality no longer match its contents - pass copies or only immutable members.
`with` returns a new object and must be captured (`quote = quote.with(tax: 0)`); the bare call is a silent no-op, and `Data` offers no setters to discover the mistake.

Nothing stops `Time.now`, `DB[...]` or `SecureRandom` inside a method that looks pure, and `attr_accessor`/`Struct`/globals re-introduce mutation; `frozen_string_literal`, review and tests are the only enforcement.

variants.name: Dry::Monads Result pipelines
variants.implementation_notes: In an application that already uses dry-rb, the core's fallible steps return `Success(...)`/`Failure(...)` values that compose with `bind`/`fmap`, so the decision sequence reads as a chain and the shell does the unwrapping (`either`, `value_or`, `failure?`); the individual steps stay plain pure methods and no exception is raised for an expected outcome. Choose it when the code base already depends on dry-monads and the decisions form a pipeline; otherwise the `Data` + `case/in` form needs no gem and no monad vocabulary.
variants.code_sketch:
include Dry::Monads[:result]

def reserve(seats:, requested:)          # pure core, dry-monads
  return Failure(:invalid_count) if requested <= 0
  return Failure(:no_capacity) if seats.taken + requested > seats.total
  Success(Seats.new(taken: seats.taken + requested))
end

# shell
reserve(seats: repo.load(id), requested: n).either(
  ->(ok)  { repo.save(id, ok) },
  ->(err) { halt 422, err.to_s })
pitfalls: A `Failure` that is never unwrapped (no `bind`, `either`, `value_or`) travels silently through the object graph; `value!` raises instead, moving the failure back into exceptions - pick one convention per code base.
Monads do not make methods pure: a `reserve` that queries the repository and then returns `Success` is still an effectful method, so keep IO in the shell and the monad for the decision flow.
Mixing `Dry::Monads` with plain `nil`-checks or exceptions leaves two error channels; convert at the boundary once (exceptions from the shell into `Failure`) instead of letting both circulate.
